questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go to an english speaking country, so that I would be going to class with domestic students rather than only exchange students. Furthermore, I wanted to go somewhere relatively far from Denmark to increase my chance at meeting different cultures. The specific university was chosen because of their very informative website and of course the many great courses they had to offer within my field.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was very easy, as the university has a student hub where you can get all the information and guidance you need face to face, rather than having to search for it online. However, the university is not good at answering e-mails. I would recommend to write to the individual professors rather than the general mail.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The O-week offers students, new or continuing, a great overview of campus and its possibilities. Furthermore, at the start of enrolment, you get some obligatory courses on Moodle that you have to complete, which is all about different procedures of the university. This really made me feel that the institution is well organised.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was surprisingly relatively easy for me. I had heard that it would be difficult, so I was searching a long time in advance. I found my accommodation through a Danish Facebook-group for exchange students going to Australia and New Zealand. We payed the rent in its entirety before arriving which is generally NOT recommended. However, the Danish students that proposed the accommodation knew someone who had lived there before, so they knew it was not a scam.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is very expensive to live in Australia and Sydney especially. If you do it the way I did, where you find something in advance it is more comfortable because you know that it is taken care of. However, if you are okay with arriving without any long term plan, you can probably find something a bit cheaper. Another thing to keep in mind is the price of accommodation vs the distance to university. If you live close to uni, it might be a bit expensive but on the other hand, you are saving money (and time) on commuting to uni. Public transport in Sydney is not very efficient and pretty expensive and Sydney is a MASSIVE city. Exchange students do not get discounts on public transport.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The process is not necessarily difficult but does have a lot of steps. First, you need to find courses in the course handbook. Then you get access to a portal where you have to apply to get accepted to each course. It is recommended that you apply for acceptance for more courses than you need, because the acceptance is not the same as secured enrolment. Some courses gets accepted right away while some take a while. Then you get access to the actual enrolment application, where you can sign up for courses. However, this is a "first come, first served" kind of deal, so you have to be fast, depending on how popular your courses are. The other issue is that the system prohibits you from applying to courses that have overlapping schedules. This can be tricky and might mean that you have to go back to the first portal and apply for another course. Once you are enrolled however, it is easy.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The website and portals are pretty intuitive and informative on their own. You also receive an email with instructions.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses I wanted except for one. The one I did not get offered a waiting list, which I did not dare to join, so I opted for quickly finding another course. However, my friend joined the waiting list and was enrolled the next day. So overall, it was not too difficult to get the courses you initially wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Use the course handbook and make a list of courses you might be interested in. Choose more than you need. In that way, you have a lot of possibilities to get what you want and not having to go back and reapply. Make sure you keep an eye on your email, so you can be ready to apply the moment the portal opens. If you are doing the summer term or another short term, be aware that there are less courses offered on these.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I took mostly first semester courses even though I was studying on my sixth semester. This was mainly due to the "prerequisites" which are the requirements you need to full fill to be able to get accepted for the course. A lot of courses from the higher levels requires you to have studied another course at UNSW. However, you can successfully (as I did for one course) argue that a course from your home university makes you eligible. 
The academic level in general is quite low/easy though. The reading is way lighter than at KU and the exams are also significantly easier. It is also very apparent that the students are much younger, as it is not unusual to start university at 17.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The professors are very personal and extremely open for student contact. It is much less academic, in the sense that it is much less formal. You as a student are often asked for your opinion rather than sticking to theory. This does take some getting used to. All my courses consisted of both lectures for the entire class, maybe 100 students, and tutorials (seminars) in smaller groups with a lot of group work.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Ways of Reasoning 
- Creating with Generative AI
- Media, Race, Politics
- Digital Studio 1

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend all of them! All of them were extremely engaging and taught me a lot of new things. My favourite was Media, Race, Politics though, as the professors were amazing and the course work was truly eye opening.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The student visa is extremely expensive, maybe 7000 kr. Furthermore, the cost of living meaning buying everday food and supplies is also very expensive. However, the university offers an assortment of free groceries once a week which was a life saver.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Generally groceries was super expensive, but asian food and asian groceries were very cheap. It was a very big hack to go to asian markets, which can be found everywhere, and buy in bulk. Coffee is cheap also.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The university has a million clubs and societies you can join which is all presented in the orientation week. You can do anything from surf-club to chess-society, to activism. There is ALWAYS something happening at campus. Furthermore, there is a regular gym, a climbing gym and a swimming pool on campus.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you attend the Paddington Campus (or not) you can take small introductions to some of their amazing art facilities and then you are free to use them in your spare time. There are photo labs, camera equipment, ceramics studio, 3D-printers and much more.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Definitely go to the Blue Mountains for hikes. Visit all the beautiful beaches. Go on a surf camp. Go to Feathersdale Zoo where you can pet wallabies and kangaroos. Go to Newtown and Marrickville.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The Australians are very friendly and very generous. It is generally a very easy society to fit into, as the people are very laid back - sometimes even too much.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It is a bit of a challenge, because almost half of all my classes were exchange students. Another difficulty is that, as stated previously, the students are much younger than the average Danish student going on exchange. I did not find many friends in my classes, but on campus in general you can find likeminded people. Take it easy - you will find your people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The age difference was probably the biggest if we are talking university. Other than that it is a very easy going culture. Sydney is super multi cultural so there are a lot of different places to go and every suburb is completely different. Take some time to try out different neighbourhoods to see where you feel like spending your time.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The diversity of the cultures you can experience. You can see the high class business people in the CBD, visit the Chinese food marked in Chinatown, be a beach babe on Bondi or go to underground techno raves in Marrickville. Sydney definitely has something for everyone.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- the university has so many opportunties outside of classes - try them out! UNSW has so many recourses compared to KU
- put what you have learned from KU a bit on standby, as they do things a bit differently. However, they are very helpful. Use your professors and don't be afraid to write them an email if you have questions
- choose some fun and exciting new courses - the university has so many to offer

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The university is beautiful and has a lot of outside areas for studying and lounging.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I think the most rewarding part was to start somewhere where you don't know anyone or anywhere and then in the end feeling a very strong connection to the place and the people.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It was a big challenge to find real friends and not just acquaintances. However, it was worthwhile.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
